sermon:
## Though You Soar Like the Eagle
*The pride that builds its nest where God cannot reach, and the God who reaches*

**Text:** Obadiah 1-9 · **Supporting:** Proverbs 16:18; Jeremiah 49:16; Isaiah 14:13-15; James 4:6

Edom built its houses in the rock. Petra, the city carved into the red cliffs of Seir, sat behind walls of stone a hundred feet high, reachable by a single narrow gorge a few men could hold against an army. You did not take Edom. You looked up at Edom and went home. And a people who cannot be taken begins, after enough generations, to say a quiet thing to itself, a thing it never says out loud, because it does not have to.

Who will bring me down.

**The wisdom of the unreachable heart**

Obadiah is the shortest book in the Old Testament, one chapter, and it opens with the LORD naming what Edom would never name about itself. "The pride of your heart has deceived you, you who live in the clefts of the rock, in your lofty dwelling, who say in your heart, 'Who will bring me down to the ground?'" (Obadiah 1:3). Hear what the prophet does. He does not begin with Edom's violence. That comes later. He begins underneath the violence, at the root, with a sentence the heart speaks to itself. The pride of your heart has deceived you. The deception is not a lie Edom tells its neighbors. It is a lie the heart tells the man, and the man believes his own heart, because the heart is the one witness we never cross-examine.

Notice where Edom located its security. In the rock. In the height. In a defensibility that was real, the cliffs were real, the gorge was real, the wise men of Teman were famous across the ancient world for counsel. "Will I not on that day, declares the LORD, destroy the wise men out of Edom, and understanding out of Mount Esau?" (Obadiah 8). Edom had altitude and Edom had intelligence, and between the two it concluded it had no need of God. That is what altitude does to a heart. It does not make you wicked first. It makes you self-sufficient first, and the wickedness follows on, because a man who needs nothing from God will eventually need nothing from his brother either.

Jeremiah, prophesying against the same nation, borrowed Obadiah's image almost word for word. "Though you make your nest as high as the eagle's, I will bring you down from there, declares the LORD" (Jeremiah 49:16). Two prophets, one verdict. The eagle's nest is the highest thing a man can build with his own hands, and the highest thing a man can build with his own hands is exactly the thing God reaches up and empties.

**The God who comes down the gorge**

Obadiah's answer to "who will bring me down" is not a debate. It is a descent. "Though you soar aloft like the eagle, though your nest is set among the stars, from there I will bring you down, declares the LORD" (Obadiah 4). The God of Israel does not argue Edom out of its height. He comes up the gorge the army could not climb. The defense that held against every nation does not slow him for a sentence, because the wall that keeps out a brother does not keep out God, and the rock you carved your house into is a rock he made.

Then the most quietly devastating line in the book. "If thieves came to you, if plunderers came by night, how you have been destroyed!, would they not steal only enough for themselves?" (Obadiah 5). A thief takes what he needs and leaves the rest. A thief, by the modest standard of his greed, shows mercy. And the LORD says Edom will be stripped lower than that. "How Esau has been pillaged, his treasures sought out!" (Obadiah 6). The nation that trusted its rock will be left with less than a burglar would have left it. Pride does not get the dignity of a robbery. Pride gets emptied to the wall.

This is the ancient pattern, older than Edom. It is Babel, a tower built to reach the heavens so a people would not be scattered, and the God who came down to the tower and scattered them anyway. It is the king of Babylon in Isaiah, the one who said in his heart, "I will ascend to heaven; above the stars of God I will set my throne on high," answered by the LORD: "But you are brought down to Sheol, to the far reaches of the pit" (Isaiah 14:13-15). The same heart, the same height, the same descent. Proverbs gave it to us as a law of the moral universe before any of these nations fell. "Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall" (Proverbs 16:18). Not pride and then, much later, after many intervening causes, destruction. Pride goes before destruction the way the front of a thing goes before the back of it. They are fastened together.

**The nest I am building**

Now turn around. I have been describing a nation in red cliffs three thousand years gone, and there is a reason that has been comfortable. Edom is safely far away. But the heart that says "who will bring me down" is not an Edomite heart. It is the human heart, and I carry one, and so do you.

Mine does not say it out loud. It says it in the budget that has no line for the possibility that I am wrong. It says it in the apology I have been owed and have decided I will collect. It says it in the strange peace I feel when a man I quietly resent has a hard year. I have stood in a pulpit and called my self-sufficiency discernment. I have built a nest out of competence and reputation and the ability to make an argument, and I have set it high enough that I do not, on most days, feel my need of God at all. That is not the absence of the sin Obadiah names. That is the sin Obadiah names, wearing a collar.

James said it with no cliff and no eagle, just the bare mechanism. "God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble" (James 4:6). Opposes. The God who reaches into the eagle's nest is not neutral toward the height we build. He is against it, actively, personally, with the full weight of his face set against the thing, and the only ground he gives grace on is ground we did not raise an inch above the valley floor.

Here is the mercy hidden in the threat. When God brings the proud man down, he is not destroying him. He is reaching him. The only place grace is given is low, and a heart that will not come down to the ground must be brought down to the ground, because God loves the proud man too much to leave him alone with his own heart in a nest among the stars. The cross is the place this stopped being a metaphor. There a King came down, not to Sheol as judgment but to a borrowed grave as mercy, and took the descent that pride had earned, so that the proud might be given the one thing the height could never buy. He went down the gorge himself.

God empties the nest to bring the man home.

## You Stood Aloof
*The day a brother bled and Edom watched, and the watching was the sin*

**Text:** Obadiah 10-14 · **Supporting:** Genesis 25:24-26; Luke 10:31-32; James 4:17; 1 John 3:17

There is a way of sinning that leaves no fingerprints. You did not strike the blow. You were not in the room when it landed. You can account for every minute, and not one of them was spent doing harm. And the LORD looks at that day, the day you did nothing, and he names it as the day of your guilt.

Edom did not invade Jerusalem. Edom watched.

**The brother in the doorway**

The charge in Obadiah is not first a charge of violence. It is a charge of relation. "Because of the violence done to your brother Jacob, shame shall cover you, and you shall be cut off forever" (Obadiah 10). Brother. The word is not poetry. Edom is Esau, and Esau is the twin of Jacob, the firstborn who came out first with the second gripping his heel (Genesis 25:24-26). These are not two nations who happened to share a border. These are the descendants of two boys who shared a womb. When Jerusalem fell, and the picture here is the Babylonian sack of 587 BC, the day the city burned and the survivors fled south through Edomite territory, Edom did not meet a stranger in distress. Edom met its brother in the doorway, bleeding, and stepped back to let him pass into worse hands.

Read what the prophet itemizes, because he refuses to let it stay general. "On the day that you stood aloof, on the day that strangers carried off his wealth and foreigners entered his gates and cast lots for Jerusalem, you were like one of them" (Obadiah 11). You stood aloof. That is the whole indictment in three words, and everything after it is God refusing to let Edom round the day off. "Do not gloat over the day of your brother in the day of his misfortune; do not rejoice over the people of Judah in the day of their ruin; do not boast in the day of distress" (Obadiah 12). Then it sharpens. "Do not enter the gate of my people in the day of their calamity; do not gloat over his disaster in the day of his calamity; do not loot his wealth in the day of his calamity" (Obadiah 13). Then it draws the line at the worst of it. "Do not stand at the crossroads to cut off his fugitives; do not hand over his survivors in the day of distress" (Obadiah 14).

Hear the escalation, because it is the anatomy of a heart that started by doing nothing. Edom stood aloof. Then Edom gloated at the standing. Then the gloating walked through the gate to loot. Then the looting went down to the crossroads to catch the ones who got away and hand them back to the killers. That is the road. It begins with a man who simply declines to help, and it ends with the same man at the fork in the road, returning the fugitive to the sword. No one starts at the crossroads. Everyone who ends at the crossroads started by standing aloof.

**The sin that has no verb**

We have a category for the harm we do. We have a much weaker category for the harm we permit, and Scripture does not share our weakness. James gives the principle stripped of all narrative. "So whoever knows the right thing to do and fails to do it, for him it is sin" (James 4:17). Sin. Not a lesser thing, not a regrettable omission, not a failure to go above and beyond. Sin, the same word for the blow as for the standing still while the blow lands. John drove it into the one place we feel it. "If anyone has the world's goods and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him, how does God's love abide in him?" (1 John 3:17). Sees. Has. Closes. The whole transaction happens without a single act. A man with means looks at a brother in need and simply lets a door inside himself swing shut, and John says God's love is not abiding in that man.

Jesus told this exact sin as a story, and we have heard it so many times we have lost the horror of it. A man lies half dead on the Jericho road. "Now by chance a priest was going down that road, and when he saw him he passed by on the other side. So likewise a Levite, when he came to the place and saw him, passed by on the other side" (Luke 10:31-32). The priest and the Levite are not the robbers. They did not beat the man. They saw the man and crossed the road, and we name them, two thousand years later, as the villains of the parable, not because of what they did, but because of what they saw and walked past. Jesus could have made the failure a thief. He made it a religious man in a hurry. Standing aloof was the sin he chose to indict, in a man who looked, on paper, clean.

**The brother I crossed the road from**

Turn the road toward us, because Obadiah will not let it stay in 587 BC and Jesus will not let it stay on the way to Jericho. The question is not whether you have harmed someone this year. Most of us, by the ledger of our actions, are reasonably clean. The question is the one Edom failed: whose calamity did you watch?

I know the marriage in my own congregation that was coming apart while I told myself it was not my business to interfere. I know the man who went quiet for two months and I noted it, the way you note weather, and did nothing, and learned later how close to the edge those two months had been. I have stood aloof and called it respecting boundaries. I have crossed the road and called it a full schedule. The most honest thing I can say about Edom is that I understand Edom from the inside, because the heart that watches a brother bleed and finds a reason to keep walking is not a foreign heart to me. It is mine on an ordinary Tuesday.

And here is where the gospel does not let us off and does not leave us condemned. There was one Brother who came to the calamity instead of standing aloof from it. Where Edom watched Jacob bleed and stepped back, Christ saw us bleeding in a calamity entirely of our own making, and he did not pass by on the other side. He crossed the whole distance, heaven to a manger to a cross, and entered the gate of our distress on the worst day, and did not hand us over to the death we had coming. He is the Samaritan who bound the wounds at his own cost. He is the Brother who would not stand aloof. The whole of the gospel is that on the day of our calamity, God did the opposite of Edom.

To stand aside is to strike.

## The Kingdom Shall Be the LORD's
*The high rock falls, Zion stands, and the last word belongs to no nation*

**Text:** Obadiah 15-21 · **Supporting:** Joel 2:32; Romans 12:19; Revelation 11:15; Philippians 2:9-11

Edom thought the story was about Edom. Most empires do. The nation in the red cliffs read its own security off the height of its rock and assumed the rock was the point. Obadiah ends by telling us the rock was never the point. The rock was a detail. The point was always a kingdom, and the kingdom was never going to be Edom's.

**The measure you used**

The book turns on a single verse, and it widens the lens from one nation to all of them. "For the day of the LORD is near upon all the nations. As you have done, it shall be done to you; your deeds shall return on your own head" (Obadiah 15). As you have done, it shall be done to you. This is not Edom's private reckoning anymore. This is the law of the day of the LORD, applied to every nation that ever stood aloof and looted and caught fugitives at the crossroads, the measure you used is the measure that comes back for you. Edom watched its brother handed over. Edom will be handed over. "And the house of Jacob shall be a fire, and the house of Joseph a flame, and the house of Esau stubble; they shall burn them and consume them, and there shall be no survivor for the house of Esau" (Obadiah 18). The nation that cut off Jacob's survivors will have no survivor. The verdict matches the crime exactly, because the God of the day of the LORD does not round off and does not forget.

We want to be careful here, because there is a counterfeit of this verse that the human heart loves. We hear "your deeds shall return on your own head" and we volunteer to be the fire. We appoint ourselves the agent of Edom's fall. But Paul tells us precisely whose hand this is. "Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, 'Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord'" (Romans 12:19). The day of the LORD is the LORD's day. The measure that returns on Edom's head returns by his judgment, not by ours, and the moment we make ourselves the flame we have become a small Edom, gloating over a brother's disaster, standing at the crossroads, doing the very thing the book condemns. The justice is real. It is not ours to carry out. It is his, and that is mercy, because his hand is just where ours is merely angry.

**Deliverance on the mountain**

Against the falling rock the prophet sets a standing mountain. "But in Mount Zion there shall be those who escape, and it shall be holy, and the house of Jacob shall possess their own possessions" (Obadiah 17). Two mountains stand opposite each other in this chapter, and the whole book has been deciding between them. Mount Esau, the high rock, the eagle's nest, brought down. Mount Zion, lower in elevation and unbreakable in fact, the place of escape and holiness and inheritance. The world measures mountains by height. God measures them by whose name is on the deed.

Obadiah did not invent that promise; he echoed it. Joel had said it of the same day: "And it shall come to pass that everyone who calls on the name of the LORD shall be saved. For in Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there shall be those who escape, as the LORD has said" (Joel 2:32). On the day every fortified nation is brought down, the only safety in the world is a called-on name on a particular mountain. Not altitude. Not a defensible gorge. Not the wisdom of Teman. A name, and a mountain that belongs to the one who answers to it.

Then the last verse of the book, and it does something we do not expect. "Saviors shall go up to Mount Zion to rule Mount Esau, and the kingdom shall be the LORD's" (Obadiah 21). Saviors go up, deliverers raised by God, ruling the very mountain that ruled itself into the ground. And then the sentence does not end on the saviors. It ends on the King. The kingdom shall be the LORD's. Not Edom's, which trusted its rock. Not Jacob's, which was looted and scattered. Not the saviors', who are sent and do not reign in their own name. The LORD's. The book that opened with a nation saying in its heart "who will bring me down" closes with the only answer that was ever true: the kingdom was never going to be yours.

**The Savior the saviors pointed to**

Now follow the saviors up the mountain, because they were always pointing past themselves. Through Israel's history, God raised deliverers, judges, kings, men who went up to rule a season and then died and left the kingdom to be lost again. Every one of them was a savior with a small s and a short shelf life, and every one of them was a finger pointing at a mountain none of them could finally hold. Obadiah's saviors on Mount Zion are a promise the Old Testament never fully cashes, because the only Savior who can go up the holy mountain and rule and not die and leave it had not yet come.

He came. He took the place of the abandoned brother, the one Edom would not stand with, and went to a worse calamity than Jerusalem's, alone, at the crossroads of the whole world's guilt, and was handed over so that we would not be. And then the descent reversed. "Therefore God has highly exalted him and bestowed on him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow" (Philippians 2:9-11). The King went up the true Zion. And John heard the end of Obadiah's sentence finished at the end of the world: "The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever" (Revelation 11:15). That is Obadiah 21 with the last veil off. The kingdom shall be the LORD's, and the LORD has a face, and the face has scars, and the throne is on a mountain no pride ever built and no army ever took.

So the book leaves us between two mountains and makes us choose which one we are standing on. I have built on Mount Esau more often than I will admit from a pulpit, on the rock of being right, the height of being needed, the wisdom of being the one with the answer. Obadiah does not let me keep that mountain. He brings it down, and he is kind to bring it down, because the only mountain that stands when the day of the LORD comes is the one I did not build and cannot lose. The question the whole chapter presses is not whether your rock is high enough. It is whose name is on your mountain.

The high rock falls; Zion stands.
